name: Sanseru
description: Sanseru means '36': 6 (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind) x 6 (color, voice, smell, taste, touch and justice). It combines Dog Kung Fu techniques with typical Goju-Ryu elements.

origin.title: Origin and History
origin.content:
Sanseru was introduced to Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned it from Ryu Ryu Ko. Originally creator unknown, likely from 'Dog Boxing' (Dog Kung Fu). Goju-ryu is the only karate style with this kata. Sanseru means '36': 6 (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind) x 6 (color, voice, smell, taste, touch and justice).

There is an important anecdote regarding Sanseru. In 1915, Chojun Miyagi traveled to Fuzhou in China, where Kanryo had lived and trained. There he met another student of Ryu Ryu Ko and he showed the katas he had learned from Kanryo, except Sanseru. The student was impressed but also said that Sanseru was missing. Miyagi said that he had learned it, but had not demonstrated it because it was his least favorite kata. Thanks to this incident, we know two important things: Kanryo learned all 9 katas from Ryu Ryu Ko and he did not remove any katas from the system.

transmission.title: Transmission to Goju-Ryu
transmission.content: Sanseru has been a fixed part of the Goju-ryu tradition from the beginning and was passed on by Miyagi Sensei to his students. Since To'on-ryu and Uechi-ryu also know it, it was presumably spread through Higaonna (and his circle). There are no major new "additions"; the kata has been unchanged in Goju from ancient times.

historicalDevelopment.title: Historical development
historicalDevelopment.content: Sanseru has the most variations of all Goju kata. The To'on-ryu version starts differently (no vertical kicks) and has different ending movements. The version of Seiko Higa also differs in details from the usual one. Modern Goju practice often follows the version of Morio Higaonna/IOGKF. An example of differences is the ending: Higaonna/Goju-kai end with two consecutive mae-geri, while Miyagi's line (Miyazato/Goju Kai) shows two tobi mae-geri. The kata is thus historically diverse in performance style.

technicalFeatures.title: Technical and philosophical characteristics
technicalFeatures.content: Sanseru is a relatively linear, straightforward kata. It uses mainly hip-twisting forward punches, powerful elbow and knee attacks, and throw/legbreak techniques. Typical elements are short close-range punch combinations and powerful bounce and kick techniques that drive the opponent to the ground. Joints, balance breaking and grips also play a role – the kata contains violent lock-like finishes and breakfalls. Philosophically it emphasizes dominance and ground techniques. The kata can be seen as a "dragon kata" (as sometimes described) in which coordinated nose-and-a-heavier attack takes place. There is no special deep breathing, rather short, explosive power.

controversy.title: Controversy/variations within Goju-Ryu
controversy.content: As mentioned, the variation is great. There is no controversy in the sense of disagreement; the fact itself is rather remarkable. Every Goju association has its own "acceptable" Sanseru. For example, in Japanese Goju-ken there are two mae-geri variants. Furthermore, Sanseru has a less dramatic finale than other kata (no formidable stance), but that is not controversial.

relationships.title: Relationship to other kata/systems
relationships.content: Sanseru is a genuine Naha-te kata and is related to kata such as Rohai and Kururunfa. Due to the emphasis on finishing punch patterns and throwing movements, it is similar to some Chinese Taiji or Dragon forms. Uechi-Ryu also has a loosely structured Sanseru-like kata (with different steps), which underscores the common origin. Symbolically, Sanseru (36) is related to Sepai (18) – it is said that 18 is half of 36, from which it would follow that Sepai is the alternative set of attacks/coverage relative to Sanseru.

modernPractice.title: Use in modern practice
modernPractice.content: Sanseru is taught as a required kata high in the Goju cycle. In training, it is used to practice various close-range techniques (claw grips, throws, wrist locks). In kata competitions, it is quite rare due to its complexity and length. However, in Goju dojos, Sanseru is a core form and is often demonstrated as an example of powerful, effective fighting.

nameAndMeaning.title: Name and meaning
nameAndMeaning.content: Sanseru (三十六步) literally means "36 steps" (sansei-ru). In the kata name "三" is three, "六" is six, and "步" is "step/hand". Most translations give "36 hands" or "36 techniques". The meaning is somewhat symbolic: 36 is a derivative of the Buddhist number 108 (108/3). It is said that numerical kata refer to initiation or acupuncture points. Sanseru can then refer to systematically going through 36 vital points or understanding all variations in one kata.

history: Sanseru is unique within the Goju curriculum: it is practiced by every Goju style and the sister system To'on-ryū and even Uechi-Ryū. This indicates that it is presumably a very old kata, before Higaonna's China trip. The transmission is unclear: the popular version of Seiko Higa (Goju Kai/Kyokushin) and that of Miyagi differ slightly. Possibly Miyagi learned Sanseru through Higaonna's fellow students (such as Juhatsu Kyoda in To'on-ryu) while Higaonna was absent. The fact is that it is a traditional Naha-te kata with Chinese influences, used by all Okinawan Goju masters.
